items.label: text
items.text: You may see other versions of this experiment recommending a different temperature rise or suggesting that you heat the water for a fixed number of minutes. There's no ideal answer to this. The higher the temperature the water reaches, the greater the heat losses during the experiment. On the other hand, if you just increase the temperature of the water by a small amount, errors in reading the thermometer or in finding the mass change of the alcohol become too significant.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Arrange the apparatus as shown in Figure 19.9 so that the spirit-burner can be used to heat the water in the copper can. The apparatus is shielded as far as possible to prevent draughts.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Light the wick to heat the water. Stop heating when you have a reasonable temperature rise of water (say, about 40.0 °C). The flame can be extinguished by putting the lid back on the wick.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Stir the water thoroughly and measure the maximum temperature of the water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Weigh the spirit-burner again with its lid on.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The experiment can be repeated with the same alcohol to check for reliability, and then carried out again with whatever other alcohols are available.

items.text: Figure 19.9 A calorimetry experiment to measure the enthalpy change of combustion of alcohols.

items.label: text
items.text: Combustion is an exothermic reaction so the temperature of the water goes up. As ethanol is burned, the total mass of the burner and ethanol goes down.

items.label: text
items.text: Using the above data we can determine how much heat is released when one mole of an alcohol is burned, that is, the molar enthalpy change of combustion.

items.label: text
items.text: We are going to use the equation Q = mc∆T so we need to find out what each quantityis.

items.label: text
items.text: Mass of water being heated = m = 100 g, the density of water is approximately 1 g/cm³ at room temperature, so 100 cm³ of water has a mass of 100 g.
